questions.stem: Which of the following apparatus is most suitable for measuring exactly 25.0 cm^3 of a solution for titration?
questions.explanation: A pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately; measuring cylinders and beakers are far less precise.

questions.stem: In an experiment to find the effect of temperature on the rate of a reaction, which of the following should be kept constant?
options: The time taken for the reaction
questions.explanation: Temperature is the independent variable and rate the dependent variable; concentration is a controlled variable.

questions.stem: The sub-atomic particle with a negligible mass and a charge of -1 is the
questions.explanation: The electron has about 1/1840 the mass of a proton and a single negative charge.

questions.stem: The nucleus of an atom contains
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons (nucleons) make up the nucleus; electrons occupy the space around it.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: An atom of an element has mass number 31 and atomic number 15. The number of neutrons in the atom is
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 31 - 15 = 16.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: The ion Al^3+ (atomic number 13, mass number 27) contains
questions.explanation: The atom has 13 electrons; losing three gives 10 electrons. Neutrons = 27 - 13 = 14.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: Chlorine consists of two isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, in the ratio 3 : 1. The relative atomic mass of chlorine is

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: An element X has two isotopes of mass numbers 63 and 65. If its relative atomic mass is 63.6, the percentage abundance of the isotope of mass 63 is

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same
questions.explanation: Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron number, so mass numbers and some physical properties differ.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a compound?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride has elements chemically combined in fixed proportion; brass and air are mixtures, sulphur is an element.

questions.topic: Particulate nature of matter: physical and chemical changes
questions.stem: Which of the following is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide) and is not easily reversed; the others are physical changes.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of an atom with atomic number 17 is
questions.explanation: 17 electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s and then five go into 3p (chlorine).

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly states Hund's rule?
options: An orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons of opposite spin.
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.
Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy.
Electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly before pairing begins.
questions.explanation: Hund's rule concerns degenerate orbitals; the second statement is Pauli's exclusion principle and the third is the Aufbau principle.

questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons that a d sub-level can hold is
questions.explanation: A d sub-level has five orbitals, each holding two electrons.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of the element with atomic number 24 (chromium) is
questions.explanation: Chromium adopts 3d5 4s1 because a half-filled d sub-level is especially stable.

questions.stem: The best method to obtain pure water from sea water is
questions.explanation: Distillation boils off the water and condenses it, leaving dissolved salts behind; filtration cannot remove dissolved solids.

questions.stem: A mixture of kerosene and water can be separated using a
questions.explanation: Kerosene and water are immiscible and form two layers that can be run off separately.

questions.stem: Which method is most suitable for separating the coloured components of a dye?
questions.explanation: Components travel at different rates on the paper because of different solubilities and adsorption.

questions.stem: Fractional distillation can be used to separate a mixture of ethanol and water because
options: the two liquids are miscible but have different boiling points.
ethanol is more dense than water.
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids whose boiling points are reasonably close (78 and 100 degrees C).

questions.stem: In paper chromatography, the R_f value of a spot that moves 3.6 cm when the solvent front moves 9.0 cm is
questions.explanation: R_f = distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent = 3.6/9.0 = 0.40.

questions.stem: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same
questions.explanation: Group number reflects the number of outer-shell electrons; period number reflects the number of shells.

questions.stem: An element with the electron configuration 2, 8, 3 belongs to
questions.explanation: Three shells means Period 3; three valence electrons means Group 3 (13). The element is aluminium.

questions.topic: Categories of elements in the periodic table
questions.stem: Which of the following elements is a metalloid?
questions.explanation: Silicon shows properties intermediate between metals and non-metals and is a semiconductor.

questions.stem: Across a period from left to right in the periodic table, the atomic radius generally
options: increases because more electrons are added.
decreases because the nuclear charge increases.
increases because the number of shells increases.
questions.explanation: Electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling the electrons closer.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy increases across a period and noble gases have very stable full shells; neon is highest here.

questions.stem: The electronegativity of the elements in Group 7 (17)
options: decreases down the group because atomic radius increases.
is the same for all the halogens.
increases down the group because the nuclear charge increases.
questions.explanation: Down the group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so attraction for bonding electrons falls.

questions.topic: Reactions of acids with metals, oxides and trioxocarbonates (IV)
questions.stem: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), the gas given off is
questions.explanation: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

questions.topic: Reactions of acids with metals, oxides and trioxocarbonates (IV)
questions.stem: Which of the following metals does NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the electrochemical series and cannot displace it from dilute acids.

questions.stem: When chlorine gas is bubbled into potassium bromide solution, the solution turns orange-brown because
options: chlorine displaces bromine from the bromide.
chlorine reacts with water to give an orange acid.
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2.

questions.topic: Elements of the first transition series
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic property of transition metals?
options: They and their compounds act as catalysts.
questions.explanation: Transition metal compounds are usually coloured, e.g. blue copper(II) sulphate and green iron(II) salts.

questions.topic: Elements of the first transition series
questions.stem: The oxidation state of manganese in KMnO4 is
questions.explanation: K is +1 and each O is -2: 1 + x - 8 = 0, so x = +7.

questions.stem: Atoms combine chemically mainly to
questions.explanation: Atoms bond by transferring or sharing electrons to achieve stable (often noble-gas) configurations.

questions.stem: Element X (2, 8, 2) combines with element Y (2, 8, 7). The formula of the compound formed is
questions.explanation: X loses two electrons (X^2+), Y gains one (Y^-), so the ionic compound is XY2.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties is typical of ionic compounds?
options: They conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.
They are soluble in organic solvents but not in water.
They conduct electricity in the solid state.
questions.explanation: Ions are fixed in the solid lattice but become mobile when melted or dissolved.

questions.stem: The bond in a hydrogen chloride molecule is
questions.explanation: H and Cl share a pair of electrons unequally because chlorine is more electronegative.

questions.stem: A dative (coordinate) covalent bond is formed when
options: delocalised electrons hold metal ions together.
electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
two atoms each contribute one electron.
both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom.
questions.explanation: Example: in NH4^+ the nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H^+.

questions.stem: The shape of the methane (CH4) molecule is
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs around carbon repel to a tetrahedral arrangement with angles of 109.5 degrees.

questions.stem: The bond angle in water (about 104.5 degrees) is smaller than in methane (109.5 degrees) because
options: lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
hydrogen bonds pull the atoms together.
questions.explanation: The two lone pairs on oxygen compress the H-O-H angle (VSEPR theory).

questions.stem: Each of the following is a triatomic molecule. Which one has a bond angle of 180 degrees?
questions.explanation: Carbon in CO2 has two double-bond regions and no lone pairs, so the molecule is linear; lone pairs on the central atom make H2O, SO2 and H2S bent.

questions.stem: Metals are good conductors of electricity because they contain
questions.explanation: In metallic bonding a 'sea' of delocalised electrons can move through the lattice of positive ions.

questions.stem: The boiling point of water is much higher than that of hydrogen sulphide because water molecules are held together by
options: only weak van der Waals forces.
questions.explanation: Highly electronegative oxygen allows strong hydrogen bonding between water molecules; sulphur does not.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the weakest intermolecular forces?
questions.explanation: Helium has only very weak van der Waals (dispersion) forces; the others are hydrogen-bonded.

questions.stem: The formula of aluminium tetraoxosulphate(VI) is
questions.explanation: Al is +3 and SO4 is -2; the lowest common multiple 6 gives Al2(SO4)3.

questions.stem: In the balanced equation a C3H8 + b O2 -> c CO2 + d H2O, the values of a, b, c and d are respectively
questions.explanation: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O: oxygen atoms on the right are 6 + 4 = 10, so 5 O2.

questions.stem: What is the relative molecular mass of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO3? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
The number of moles in 8.8 g of carbon(IV) oxide (CO2) is (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CO2 = 44 g/mol; n = 8.8/44 = 0.20 mol.

questions.stem: How many molecules are present in 3.6 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16; Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1)
A compound has the empirical formula CH2O and a relative molecular mass of 180. Its molecular formula is
questions.explanation: Empirical formula mass = 30; 180/30 = 6, so (CH2O)6 = C6H12O6.

questions.stem: The percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium trioxonitrate(V), NH4NO3, is (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: M = 80; mass of N = 28; percentage = 28/80 x 100 = 35%.

questions.stem: What mass of magnesium oxide is formed when 6.0 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen? (Mg = 24, O = 16)
questions.explanation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO: 24 g Mg gives 40 g MgO, so 6.0 g gives 10 g.

questions.stem: What volume of carbon(IV) oxide, measured at s.t.p., is produced when 25 g of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) is completely decomposed by heat? (CaCO3 = 100; molar volume = 22.4 dm^3)
questions.explanation: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. 25 g = 0.25 mol, giving 0.25 mol CO2 = 5.6 dm^3.

questions.stem: Calculate the mass of iron produced when 16 g of iron(III) oxide is completely reduced: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (Fe = 56, O = 16)
questions.explanation: M(Fe2O3) = 160; 16 g = 0.10 mol, giving 0.20 mol Fe = 11.2 g.

questions.stem: A solution contains 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide in 500 cm^3 of solution. Its concentration in mol/dm^3 is (NaOH = 40)
A standard solution is a solution
options: that contains one mole of solute in 1 dm^3 of water.
that is saturated at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Any solution of accurately known concentration is a standard solution; it need not be 1 mol/dm^3.

questions.stem: What volume of 2.0 mol/dm^3 hydrochloric acid is needed to prepare 500 cm^3 of 0.10 mol/dm^3 acid?
50 cm^3 of water is added to 150 cm^3 of 0.40 mol/dm^3 sodium chloride solution. The concentration of the new solution is
questions.explanation: Moles are unchanged: 0.40 x 150/200 = 0.30 mol/dm^3.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the particles of a solid
options: are far apart with no forces between them.
are completely at rest at all temperatures.
questions.explanation: Strong forces hold solid particles in fixed positions, about which they vibrate.

questions.stem: The direct change of a solid to vapour on heating, without passing through the liquid state, is called
questions.explanation: Iodine and ammonium chloride sublime on heating; evaporation is liquid to vapour.

questions.stem: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas are released at opposite ends of a long glass tube. A white ring of ammonium chloride forms
options: at both ends of the tube.
nearer the ammonia end, because hydrogen chloride diffuses faster.
exactly at the middle of the tube.
nearer the hydrogen chloride end, because ammonia diffuses faster.
questions.explanation: NH3 (17) is lighter than HCl (36.5) and diffuses faster, so the gases meet nearer the HCl end.

questions.stem: Under the same conditions, the rate of diffusion of methane (CH4) compared with that of sulphur(IV) oxide (SO2) is (C = 12, H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Rate is inversely proportional to sqrt(M): rate(CH4)/rate(SO2) = sqrt(64/16) = 2.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 300 cm^3 at 27 degrees C and 760 mmHg. What will its volume be at s.t.p. (0 degrees C, 760 mmHg)?
questions.explanation: V2 = 300 x 273/300 = 273 cm^3 (pressure unchanged).

questions.stem: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which
options: its saturated vapour pressure equals the external atmospheric pressure.
questions.explanation: Evaporation takes place at all temperatures; boiling occurs when s.v.p. equals the external pressure.

questions.stem: The difference between a vapour and a gas is that a vapour
options: always has a higher density than a liquid.
can be liquefied by pressure alone because it is below its critical temperature.
questions.explanation: A vapour is a gaseous substance below its critical temperature, so compression alone can liquefy it.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride crystals are hard and have high melting points because
options: weak van der Waals forces hold the molecules together.
strong electrostatic forces hold the ions in a giant lattice.
the molecules are joined by hydrogen bonds.
questions.explanation: Ionic lattices require much energy to separate oppositely charged ions.

questions.stem: Graphite is used as a lubricant and as electrodes because
options: it is the hardest substance known.
it has layers that slide over one another and has delocalised electrons.
each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds.
questions.explanation: Weak forces between layers allow sliding; the fourth electron of each carbon is delocalised, allowing conduction.

questions.stem: Diamond and graphite are
questions.explanation: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: SiO2 is a giant covalent (macromolecular) solid; iodine, naphthalene and sulphur are simple molecular solids with weak intermolecular forces.

questions.stem: A reaction in which heat is given out to the surroundings is described as
options: exothermic, with a positive enthalpy change.
endothermic, with a positive enthalpy change.
exothermic, with a negative enthalpy change.
endothermic, with a negative enthalpy change.
questions.explanation: In exothermic reactions the products have less energy than the reactants, so Delta H is negative.

questions.stem: When 1.6 g of methane (CH4) is burnt completely, 89 kJ of heat is released. The enthalpy of combustion of methane is (C = 12, H = 1)

When 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol/dm^3 HCl is mixed with 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol/dm^3 NaOH, the temperature rises by 6.8 degrees C. Assuming the solution has a specific heat capacity of 4.2 J/g K and a density of 1.0 g/cm^3, the heat of neutralisation is approximately
questions.explanation: Heat = 100 x 4.2 x 6.8 = 2856 J for 0.050 mol water formed; Delta H = -2856/0.050 = -57 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction is most likely to be spontaneous when
options: Delta H is negative and Delta S is positive.
Delta H is positive and Delta S is negative.
Delta H and Delta S are both zero.
questions.explanation: Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S is then negative at all temperatures.

questions.stem: For a reaction, Delta H = +40 kJ/mol and Delta S = +0.16 kJ/mol K. Above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous when Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S < 0, i.e. T > 40/0.16 = 250 K.

questions.stem: According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory, an acid is a substance that
questions.explanation: Bronsted-Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a property of alkalis?
options: They react with metals to give hydrogen in all cases.
questions.explanation: Alkalis are bitter and soapy and turn red litmus blue.

questions.topic: Acids, bases and salts as electrolytes
questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is described as a weak acid because it
options: is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.
questions.explanation: Strength refers to degree of ionisation, not concentration.

questions.stem: The basicity of tetraoxophosphate(V) acid, H3PO4, is
questions.explanation: Basicity is the number of replaceable hydrogen ions per molecule of acid; H3PO4 has three.

questions.stem: A solution with a pH of 2 is
questions.explanation: pH values well below 7 indicate strong acidity; pH 7 is neutral.

questions.stem: The pH of a 0.01 mol/dm^3 solution of hydrochloric acid (fully ionised) is
The pH of a 0.001 mol/dm^3 solution of sodium hydroxide at 25 degrees C is
A salt formed by the partial replacement of the ionisable hydrogen of an acid by a metal is
questions.explanation: Example: sodium hydrogen tetraoxosulphate(VI), NaHSO4.

questions.stem: An insoluble salt such as barium tetraoxosulphate(VI) is best prepared by
options: titration of an acid and an alkali.
questions.explanation: Mixing solutions of a soluble barium salt and a soluble sulphate precipitates BaSO4, which is filtered, washed and dried.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is
options: neutral, because it is a salt.
acidic, because NH4^+ ions are hydrolysed to release H^+ ions.
alkaline, because Cl^- ions are hydrolysed.
questions.explanation: NH4Cl is the salt of a strong acid and a weak base; NH4^+ + H2O <=> NH3 + H3O^+.

questions.stem: Which of the following salts gives an alkaline solution in water?
questions.explanation: Na2CO3 is the salt of a strong base and a weak acid; CO3^2- hydrolyses to give OH^- ions.

questions.stem: A substance that absorbs moisture from the atmosphere and dissolves in it to form a solution is said to be
questions.explanation: Deliquescent substances such as calcium chloride and sodium hydroxide pellets absorb enough water to dissolve.

questions.stem: The most suitable indicator for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution is
questions.explanation: For a weak acid against a strong base the end point is alkaline (pH about 8-10), matching phenolphthalein's range.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.10 mol/dm^3 sodium hydroxide solution required 20.0 cm^3 of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. The concentration of the acid is
questions.explanation: NaOH + HCl react 1 : 1: C(acid) = 0.10 x 25.0/20.0 = 0.125 mol/dm^3.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm^3 of sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) solution required 20.0 cm^3 of 0.10 mol/dm^3 H2SO4 for complete neutralisation. The concentration of the Na2CO3 solution is
questions.explanation: Na2CO3 + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2 (1 : 1). Moles of acid = 0.002; C = 0.002/0.025 = 0.080 mol/dm^3.

questions.stem: A solution that contains as much solute as it can dissolve at a given temperature in the presence of undissolved solute is
questions.explanation: A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute at that temperature.

questions.stem: The solubility of a salt at 30 degrees C is 0.50 mol/dm^3. If its molar mass is 74.5 g/mol, the mass of the salt that will saturate 200 cm^3 of water at that temperature is approximately

When a saturated solution of potassium trioxonitrate(V) containing 110 g of the salt per 100 g of water at 60 degrees C is cooled to 20 degrees C, 78 g of crystals are deposited from 100 g of water. The solubility at 20 degrees C in g per 100 g water is
questions.explanation: Mass remaining dissolved = 110 - 78 = 32 g per 100 g of water.

questions.stem: Fizzy soft drinks release bubbles when the bottle is opened because
options: the temperature of the drink rises suddenly.
the pressure is reduced, lowering the solubility of carbon(IV) oxide.
oxygen from the air reacts with the drink.
questions.explanation: The CO2 was dissolved under pressure; opening reduces pressure and the excess gas comes out of solution.

questions.stem: The rate of a chemical reaction can be measured by
options: the total mass of the reactants.
the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
the colour of the final products.
the number of reactants in the equation.
questions.explanation: Rate is the change of amount or concentration of a substance per unit time.

questions.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than marble chips of the same mass because the powder has
questions.explanation: More surface is exposed for collisions between acid particles and the solid.

questions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
options: shifting the equilibrium position to the right.
providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
increasing the enthalpy change of the reaction.
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation energy, allowing more collisions to be effective; it does not change Delta H or the equilibrium position.

questions.stem: According to the collision theory, raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction mainly because
options: more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
the concentration of the reactants increases.
the products are formed with less energy.
questions.explanation: Higher temperature shifts the energy distribution so a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

questions.stem: In an experiment, 60 cm^3 of hydrogen was collected in the first 20 s and a total of 90 cm^3 in the first 40 s. The average rate of reaction between 20 s and 40 s is
A chemical system is said to be in dynamic equilibrium when
options: all the reactants have been converted to products.
the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction.
the concentrations of reactants and products are always equal.
questions.explanation: Both reactions continue at equal rates so concentrations remain constant (but not necessarily equal).

questions.stem: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), Delta H = -92 kJ/mol, the yield of ammonia is increased by
questions.explanation: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 versus 4). Higher temperature favours the endothermic back reaction.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), Delta H negative, which change will shift the equilibrium to the LEFT?
questions.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating favours the endothermic backward reaction.

questions.stem: Oxidation can be defined as
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons (or increase in oxidation number); reduction is gain of electrons.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, the species that is oxidised is
questions.explanation: Zn loses two electrons to become Zn^2+; Cu^2+ gains them and is reduced.

questions.stem: The oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7 is
In the reaction H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, hydrogen sulphide acts as
questions.explanation: Sulphur goes from -2 to 0 (oxidised), so H2S donates electrons and is the reducing agent.

questions.stem: Which of the following can act as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent?
questions.explanation: S in SO2 is +4 and can be oxidised to +6 or reduced to 0; Na only reduces, F2 and KMnO4 only oxidise.

questions.stem: When acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) acts as an oxidising agent, its colour changes from
questions.explanation: Cr2O7^2- (orange) is reduced to Cr^3+ (green); purple to colourless is the change for MnO4^-.

questions.stem: In the balanced ionic equation MnO4^- + 8H^+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe^3+, the number of electrons gained by each MnO4^- ion is
questions.explanation: Mn changes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons; hence 5 Fe^2+ ions are oxidised.

questions.stem: In a Daniell cell (Zn | Zn^2+ || Cu^2+ | Cu), electrons flow in the external circuit from
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised at the anode (negative electrode) and its electrons travel to the copper cathode.

questions.stem: Given the standard electrode potentials Zn^2+/Zn = -0.76 V and Cu^2+/Cu = +0.34 V, the e.m.f. of the cell Zn | Zn^2+ || Cu^2+ | Cu is
During electrolysis, the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the battery is the
questions.explanation: Anions move to the anode and lose electrons there (oxidation).

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid using platinum electrodes, the volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen produced is
questions.explanation: 4H^+ + 4e^- -> 2H2 at the cathode while 4OH^- -> 2H2O + O2 + 4e^- at the anode; 2 mol H2 for each mol O2.

questions.stem: When concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine) is electrolysed using carbon electrodes, the product at the anode is
questions.explanation: Although OH^- is lower in the series, the high concentration of Cl^- causes chlorine to be discharged.

questions.stem: What mass of copper is deposited at the cathode when a current of 2.0 A is passed through copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution for 1 hour 20 minutes 25 seconds? (Cu = 64; F = 96 500 C/mol)

The same quantity of electricity is passed through solutions of silver trioxonitrate(V) and copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) in series. If 10.8 g of silver is deposited, the mass of copper deposited is (Ag = 108, Cu = 64)
questions.explanation: 10.8 g Ag = 0.10 mol, needing 0.10 F; this deposits 0.050 mol Cu = 3.2 g.

questions.stem: In electroplating a steel spoon with silver, the spoon is made the
options: anode, in a solution of a silver salt.
cathode, in a solution of an iron salt.
cathode, in a solution of a silver salt.
questions.explanation: Ag^+ ions are reduced and deposited on the cathode; a silver anode replaces them.

questions.stem: The rusting of iron requires
questions.explanation: Experiments show iron does not rust in dry air or in boiled water free of air.

questions.stem: Zinc protects galvanised iron from rusting even when the coating is scratched because zinc
options: is more reactive than iron and corrodes in preference (sacrificial protection).
questions.explanation: Zinc is higher in the electrochemical series, so it loses electrons instead of the iron.

questions.stem: The general formula of the alkanes is
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated: e.g. CH4, C2H6, C3H8.

questions.stem: Members of a homologous series
options: differ from one another by a CH2 group.
questions.explanation: Members share a general formula and functional group and show a gradation in physical properties.

questions.stem: The functional group in alkanols is
questions.explanation: Alkanols contain the hydroxyl group; -COOH is the carboxyl group of alkanoic acids.

questions.topic: Separation and purification of organic compounds
questions.stem: The purity of a solid organic compound is best checked by determining its
questions.explanation: A pure solid melts sharply at a definite temperature; impurities lower and broaden the melting range.

questions.stem: Crude oil is separated into its fractions by
questions.explanation: Fractions with different boiling ranges condense at different heights in the fractionating column.

questions.stem: Cracking of long-chain hydrocarbons is carried out mainly to
options: produce more petrol and alkenes from heavy fractions.
increase the boiling point of petrol.
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks large, less useful molecules into smaller alkanes (for petrol) and alkenes (for plastics).

questions.stem: The octane rating of petrol is a measure of its
options: resistance to knocking in the engine.
questions.explanation: Petrol with a high octane number burns smoothly without premature ignition (knocking); 2,2,4-trimethylpentane is rated 100.

questions.stem: Which of the following fractions of crude oil has the highest boiling range?
questions.explanation: Bitumen contains the largest molecules and is the residue at the bottom of the column.

questions.topic: Determination of formulae and structures of organic compounds
questions.stem: 0.30 g of an organic compound containing C, H and O only gave 0.44 g of CO2 and 0.18 g of H2O on complete combustion. Its empirical formula is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
Which of the following is a general property of organic compounds?
options: They are mostly ionic with high melting points.
They dissolve readily in water and conduct electricity.
They are usually covalent and burn readily.
questions.explanation: Most organic compounds are covalent, have low melting points, are flammable and dissolve better in organic solvents.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light by
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated; a hydrogen atom is replaced by chlorine to give CH3Cl and HCl.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is
questions.explanation: The longest chain has 4 carbons with a methyl on carbon 2 (lowest locant).

questions.stem: Ethene decolourises bromine water because it
options: undergoes an addition reaction across the double bond.
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across C=C to form colourless 1,2-dibromoethane; this is the test for unsaturation.

questions.stem: Ethene can be prepared in the laboratory by heating ethanol with
options: excess concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid at about 170 degrees C.
dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates ethanol to ethene; dichromate would oxidise it.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of nickel catalyst at about 150 degrees C to form
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation adds H2 across the double bond; the same process hardens vegetable oils to margarine.

questions.stem: Ethyne is prepared in the laboratory by the action of water on
questions.explanation: CaC2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + C2H2.

questions.stem: The oxy-ethyne (oxyacetylene) flame is used for welding and cutting metals because
options: it has a very high temperature.
questions.explanation: The combustion of ethyne in oxygen produces temperatures of about 3000 degrees C.

questions.stem: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions mainly because
options: its delocalised pi-electron system is very stable.
it contains three isolated double bonds.
questions.explanation: Addition would destroy the stable delocalised (aromatic) ring, so substitution preserving the ring is preferred.

questions.stem: The molecular formula of benzene is
questions.explanation: Benzene is a planar six-membered ring with one hydrogen on each carbon.

questions.stem: The alkanol present in palm wine and produced by the fermentation of sugars is
questions.explanation: Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon(IV) oxide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a secondary alkanol?
questions.explanation: In propan-2-ol the -OH carbon is attached to two other carbons; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.

questions.stem: When ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI), it is oxidised first to ethanal and then to
questions.explanation: Primary alkanols are oxidised to alkanals and then alkanoic acids.

questions.stem: The acid in vinegar is
questions.explanation: Vinegar is a dilute solution (about 4-8%) of ethanoic acid.

options: sodium ethanoate, water and carbon(IV) oxide.
questions.explanation: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2: a typical acid-carbonate reaction.

questions.topic: Alkanoates as derivatives of alkanoic acids
questions.stem: The reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 is called
questions.explanation: It produces the ester ethyl ethanoate and water.

questions.topic: Alkanoates as derivatives of alkanoic acids
questions.stem: The ester formed from methanoic acid and propan-1-ol is
questions.explanation: Esters are named alkyl (from the alcohol) + alkanoate (from the acid): HCOOCH2CH2CH3 is propyl methanoate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a heavy chemical produced in large tonnage?
questions.explanation: Heavy chemicals such as H2SO4, NaOH and ammonia are made in very large quantities; fine chemicals in small amounts.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is LEAST important in siting a cement factory?
questions.explanation: Raw materials, power, transport and labour are key siting factors; tourist attractions are not.

questions.stem: Which of the following gases is mainly responsible for acid rain?
questions.explanation: SO2 (and nitrogen oxides) dissolve in rain water to form acids.

questions.stem: Gas flaring in the Niger Delta contributes to global warming mainly by releasing
questions.explanation: Burning associated gas produces CO2, and incomplete flaring releases methane; both are greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: Carbon(II) oxide is dangerous to humans because it
options: is a strong acid that burns the lungs.
combines with haemoglobin to form a stable compound, reducing oxygen transport.
causes the ozone layer to thicken.
questions.explanation: CO is colourless and odourless; carboxyhaemoglobin prevents haemoglobin from carrying oxygen. Running generators indoors is therefore deadly.

questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are harmful to the environment because they
options: release chlorine atoms that destroy the ozone layer.
questions.explanation: UV light breaks CFCs, releasing Cl atoms that catalyse the breakdown of ozone.

questions.stem: The production of ethanol from sugar solutions using yeast is an example of
questions.explanation: Yeast enzymes (zymase) convert glucose to ethanol and CO2 under anaerobic conditions.

questions.stem: Proteins are polymers formed from
options: glucose units joined by glycosidic links.
amino acids joined by peptide linkages.
questions.explanation: The -CO-NH- (peptide or amide) linkage joins amino acid units.

questions.stem: When a protein solution is warmed with sodium hydroxide and a few drops of dilute copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution, a violet colour indicates
options: the presence of a reducing sugar.
the presence of peptide bonds (Biuret test).
questions.explanation: The Biuret test gives a violet/purple colour with proteins.

questions.stem: Amino acids are amphoteric because they contain
options: both an amino group and a carboxyl group.
a hydroxyl group and a carbonyl group.
questions.explanation: The -NH2 group can accept a proton (basic) and the -COOH group can donate one (acidic).

questions.stem: Soap is produced by boiling fats or oils with sodium hydroxide solution. This process is called
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats gives glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids (soap).

questions.stem: In the manufacture of margarine, liquid groundnut oil is hardened into a soft solid by
options: hydrogenation in the presence of a nickel catalyst.
questions.explanation: Adding hydrogen to the C=C bonds raises the melting point, making the oil solid at room temperature.

questions.stem: The reagent used to test for starch is
questions.explanation: Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reducing sugar that gives a brick-red precipitate with Fehling's solution?
questions.explanation: Glucose has a free aldehyde (reducing) group; sucrose, starch and cellulose do not reduce Fehling's solution.

questions.explanation: Starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose units only.

questions.stem: Polyethene is formed from ethene by
questions.explanation: Ethene molecules join through their double bonds without loss of any small molecule.

questions.explanation: Nylon forms with loss of water (or HCl) between diamine and diacid (or diacyl chloride) monomers.

questions.explanation: Bakelite has a cross-linked structure and does not soften on reheating; the others are thermoplastics.

questions.stem: Carbon(IV) oxide is used in fire extinguishers because it
options: is denser than air and does not support combustion.
questions.explanation: It blankets the fire, cutting off oxygen.

questions.stem: The test for carbon(IV) oxide is that it
questions.explanation: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 (white precipitate) + H2O.

questions.explanation: 2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2, catalysed by MnO2.

questions.explanation: Examples include zinc oxide and aluminium oxide.

questions.explanation: Na2CO3 precipitates Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ as insoluble trioxocarbonates(IV); boiling removes only temporary hardness.

questions.stem: In the treatment of town water supply, chlorine is added to
questions.explanation: Chlorination disinfects water; alum is used for coagulating suspended particles.

options: reacts with water to form oxochlorate(I) acid, which releases oxygen.

options: remove hydrogen chloride and then dry the gas.

questions.stem: Ammonia gas is dried using
questions.explanation: Ammonia is basic and reacts with H2SO4 and P4O10 and forms a complex with CaCl2.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, the conditions commonly used are
options: about 200 atm, 450 degrees C and an iron catalyst.
1 atm, 25 degrees C and a platinum catalyst.
200 atm, 1000 degrees C and no catalyst.
2 atm, 450 degrees C and a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
questions.explanation: These are compromise conditions for yield and rate; V2O5 is the catalyst in the Contact process.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the test for ammonia gas?
options: It turns damp red litmus paper blue.
questions.explanation: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas; it also forms white fumes with HCl.

questions.stem: In the Contact process, sulphur(VI) oxide is absorbed in concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid rather than water because

water would reduce SO3 to sulphur.
direct reaction with water produces a fine mist of acid that is difficult to condense.

questions.explanation: 2SO2 + O2 <=> 2SO3 over V2O5 at about 450 degrees C.

questions.stem: The noble gases are unreactive because
options: their outermost shells are completely filled (stable octet or duplet).

questions.stem: Argon is used in electric light bulbs because it
options: is a good conductor of electricity.
is inert and does not react with the hot filament.

questions.stem: Aluminium is extracted from purified bauxite by
options: electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite.
reduction with carbon in a blast furnace.

questions.explanation: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Limestone removes silica impurities as slag.

options: remove silica impurities as calcium trioxosilicate(IV) (slag).
questions.explanation: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (slag).

questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of
questions.explanation: Bronze is copper and tin; steel is iron and carbon; solder is lead and tin.

questions.stem: Duralumin is used in making aircraft bodies mainly because it is
questions.explanation: Duralumin (aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese) has a high strength-to-weight ratio.

questions.stem: Sodium is stored under paraffin oil because it
options: reacts readily with air and water.
is a liquid at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Sodium tarnishes rapidly in air and reacts vigorously with water.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide is manufactured industrially by
questions.explanation: Electrolysis of concentrated NaCl solution gives NaOH, chlorine and hydrogen. The Solvay process makes Na2CO3.

questions.stem: Plaster of Paris sets into a hard mass when mixed with water because it
options: takes up water to form gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O).
questions.explanation: (CaSO4)2.H2O + 3H2O -> 2CaSO4.2H2O, which sets hard; it is used for casts.

questions.explanation: Heating limestone gives quicklime (CaO); adding water gives slaked lime, Ca(OH)2.

options: it is covered by a thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide.
it is below hydrogen in the series.

questions.stem: Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give
questions.explanation: Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2; hydrogen produced keeps iron in the +2 state.

questions.stem: When copper turnings are added to concentrated trioxonitrate(V) acid, the brown gas evolved is
questions.explanation: Cu + 4HNO3(conc) -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O. Dilute acid gives colourless NO.

questions.explanation: It takes up water of crystallisation to form blue CuSO4.5H2O.

remove air bubbles from the tip.

Add water quickly to the acid.
Add the acid slowly to the water with stirring.
Mix them in a closed container.

questions.explanation: Flame colours: sodium golden yellow, potassium lilac, calcium brick red, copper blue-green.

questions.explanation: BaSO4 is insoluble in dilute HCl; BaCO3 and BaSO3 dissolve with effervescence.

questions.topic: Atomic number, isotopes and atomic mass
questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) atomic number; (ii) mass number; (iii) isotopy. [6 marks]
(b) Silicon occurs naturally as three isotopes: 28Si (92.0%), 29Si (5.0%) and 30Si (3.0%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon. [3 marks]
(c) Write the electron configuration (s, p, d notation) of (i) magnesium (atomic number 12); (ii) chlorine (atomic number 17); (iii) potassium (atomic number 19). [3 marks]
(d) State (i) the Aufbau principle; (ii) Pauli's exclusion principle. [4 marks]
(e) Give three differences between a proton and an electron. [3 marks]
(f) Describe how a mixture of sand, common salt and iodine crystals can be separated into its components. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Atomic number: the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
2 marks: Mass number: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
2 marks: Isotopy: the existence of atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers
1 mark: R.A.M. = (92.0 x 28 + 5.0 x 29 + 3.0 x 30)/100
1 mark: = (2576 + 145 + 90)/100
1 mark: = 28.11 (about 28.1)
1 mark: Mg: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2
1 mark: Cl: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5
1 mark: K: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1
2 marks: Aufbau: electrons occupy orbitals in order of increasing energy, lowest energy first
2 marks: Pauli: no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers / an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin
3 marks: Any three, 1 mark each: proton is positive, electron negative; proton is about 1840 times heavier; proton is in the nucleus, electron outside it; proton number defines the element
2 marks: Heat the mixture gently: iodine sublimes and is collected on a cold surface (e.g. a cold funnel or flask)
2 marks: Add water to the residue and stir: salt dissolves; filter to remove sand as residue, then wash and dry the sand
2 marks: Evaporate the filtrate to dryness (or crystallise) to recover the salt
questions.explanation: (a) Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; isotopy = same element, different mass numbers. (b) R.A.M. = 28.11. (c) Mg 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2; Cl ...3s2 3p5; K ...3p6 4s1. (d) Aufbau: lowest energy first; Pauli: no two electrons share four quantum numbers. (e) Charge, mass, location. (f) Sublime iodine, dissolve salt and filter off sand, evaporate filtrate for salt.

questions.stem:
(a) State the periodic law. [2 marks]
(b) Elements P, Q, R and S have atomic numbers 11, 12, 17 and 18 respectively.
(i) Write the electron configuration of each element. [4 marks]
(ii) To which group and period does R belong? [2 marks]
(iii) Which of the elements is the most reactive metal? Give a reason. [2 marks]
(iv) Which element is chemically unreactive? Explain. [2 marks]
(v) Write the formula of the compound formed between Q and R and state the type of bonding. [3 marks]
(c) Explain the trend in (i) atomic radius across a period; (ii) first ionisation energy down a group. [6 marks]
(d) Give two physical and two chemical differences between metals and non-metals. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: The properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers
4 marks: P: 2,8,1; Q: 2,8,2; R: 2,8,7; S: 2,8,8 (1 mark each)
1 mark: R is in Group 7 (17)
1 mark: Period 3
1 mark: P (sodium) is the most reactive metal
1 mark: It has one valence electron that it loses most easily
1 mark: S (argon) is unreactive
1 mark: Its outer shell is complete (stable octet)
1 mark: Formula QR2 (MgCl2)
1 mark: Ionic (electrovalent) bonding
1 mark: Q transfers two electrons, one to each R atom
1 mark: Atomic radius decreases across a period
1 mark: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
1 mark: so the outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus
1 mark: First ionisation energy decreases down a group
1 mark: Atomic radius and the number of inner shells increase (more shielding)
1 mark: so the outer electron is held less firmly and removed more easily
2 marks: Physical, any two (1 mark each): metals are lustrous, malleable/ductile, good conductors, usually high melting point; non-metals are dull, brittle, poor conductors
2 marks: Chemical, any two (1 mark each): metals form basic oxides, form positive ions, liberate hydrogen from dilute acids; non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides, form negative ions
questions.explanation: (a) Properties are a periodic function of atomic number. (b)(i) 2,8,1; 2,8,2; 2,8,7; 2,8,8. (ii) Group 7, Period 3. (iii) P loses its single valence electron most easily. (iv) S has a full octet. (v) QR2, ionic. (c) Radius falls across a period as nuclear charge rises; ionisation energy falls down a group as radius and shielding increase. (d) Metals lustrous, malleable, conductors, basic oxides; non-metals brittle, insulators, acidic oxides.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain with an example each: (i) ionic bond; (ii) covalent bond; (iii) dative covalent bond. [6 marks]
(b) Using the valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory, predict and explain the shapes of (i) CH4; (ii) NH3; (iii) H2O. Give the approximate bond angle in each. [9 marks]
(c) Explain why (i) water has a higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide; (ii) graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. [6 marks]
(d) State four properties of covalent compounds. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Ionic bond: formed by transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
1 mark: Example: NaCl / MgO
1 mark: Covalent bond: formed by sharing of electron pairs between atoms
1 mark: Example: H2, Cl2, CH4
1 mark: Dative bond: a shared pair in which both electrons are donated by one atom
1 mark: Example: NH4^+ or H3O^+
1 mark: CH4: four bonding pairs, no lone pair
1 mark: Tetrahedral
1 mark: 109.5 degrees
1 mark: NH3: three bonding pairs and one lone pair
1 mark: Trigonal pyramidal
1 mark: About 107 degrees, because lone pair-bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair-bond pair repulsion
1 mark: H2O: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs
1 mark: Bent (V-shaped)
1 mark: About 104.5 degrees, as two lone pairs compress the angle further
1 mark: Oxygen is much more electronegative than sulphur
1 mark: so hydrogen bonds form between water molecules
1 mark: more energy is needed to separate them, giving a higher boiling point
1 mark: In graphite each carbon is bonded to only three others
1 mark: leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move between the layers and carry current
1 mark: In diamond all four valence electrons are used in bonding, so there are no mobile electrons
4 marks: Any four, 1 mark each: low melting and boiling points; mostly insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents; non-conductors of electricity; often volatile; exist as molecules (gases, liquids or soft solids)
questions.explanation: (a) Ionic: electron transfer (NaCl); covalent: sharing (Cl2); dative: both electrons from one atom (NH4^+). (b) CH4 tetrahedral 109.5; NH3 pyramidal 107; H2O bent 104.5, due to lone-pair repulsion. (c) Hydrogen bonding in water; delocalised electrons in graphite. (d) Low m.p., non-conductors, soluble in organic solvents, volatile.

questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) the mole; (ii) molar volume of a gas at s.t.p. [4 marks]
(b) State (i) Avogadro's law; (ii) the law of conservation of mass. [4 marks]
(c) 12.5 g of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) reacted completely with 2.0 mol/dm^3 hydrochloric acid according to the equation:
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
Calculate:
(i) the number of moles of CaCO3 used; [2 marks]
(ii) the volume of carbon(IV) oxide produced at s.t.p.; [3 marks]
(iii) the minimum volume of the acid required; [3 marks]
(iv) the mass of calcium chloride formed. [3 marks]
[Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16, Cl = 35.5; molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3]
(d) A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass, and its relative molecular mass is 60. Determine its molecular formula. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Mole: the amount of substance that contains as many elementary particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12 (6.02 x 10^23 particles)
2 marks: Molar volume: the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at s.t.p., i.e. 22.4 dm^3
2 marks: Avogadro: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules
2 marks: Conservation of mass: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction / total mass of reactants equals total mass of products
1 mark: M(CaCO3) = 100 g/mol
1 mark: n = 12.5/100 = 0.125 mol
1 mark: Mole ratio CaCO3 : CO2 = 1 : 1
1 mark: n(CO2) = 0.125 mol; V = 0.125 x 22.4
1 mark: = 2.80 dm^3
1 mark: n(HCl) = 2 x 0.125 = 0.250 mol
1 mark: V = n/C = 0.250/2.0 = 0.125 dm^3
1 mark: = 125 cm^3
1 mark: M(CaCl2) = 40 + 71 = 111 g/mol
1 mark: mass = 0.125 x 111
1 mark: = 13.9 g (13.875 g)
1 mark: C: 40.0/12 = 3.33; H: 6.7/1 = 6.7; O: 53.3/16 = 3.33
1 mark: Divide by smallest: 1 : 2 : 1
1 mark: Empirical formula CH2O
1 mark: Empirical formula mass = 30
1 mark: n = 60/30 = 2
1 mark: Molecular formula C2H4O2
questions.explanation: (a) Mole = Avogadro number of particles; molar volume = 22.4 dm^3 at s.t.p. (b) Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules; mass is conserved. (c)(i) 0.125 mol. (ii) 2.80 dm^3. (iii) 125 cm^3. (iv) 13.9 g. (d) CH2O x 2 = C2H4O2.

questions.stem:
(a) State four assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases. [4 marks]
(b) State (i) Charles's law; (ii) Graham's law of diffusion. [4 marks]
(c) A gas occupies 200 cm^3 at 27 degrees C and 750 mmHg. Calculate its volume at s.t.p. (0 degrees C and 760 mmHg). [4 marks]
(d) Under the same conditions, a given volume of hydrogen diffuses through a porous pot in 20 s. How long will the same volume of oxygen take to diffuse? (H = 1, O = 16) [4 marks]
(e) Explain, in terms of the kinetic theory, why (i) a gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container; (ii) the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated at constant volume. [4 marks]
(f) Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressures and low temperatures. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Any four, 1 mark each: gases consist of tiny particles in constant random motion; the volume of the particles is negligible compared with that of the container; there are no forces of attraction or repulsion between particles; collisions are perfectly elastic; average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature
2 marks: Charles: the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature at constant pressure
2 marks: Graham: at constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density (or molar mass)
1 mark: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2
1 mark: V2 = 200 x 750 x 273/(300 x 760)
1 mark: Correct substitution with temperatures in kelvin (300 K and 273 K)
1 mark: V2 = 179.6 cm^3 (about 180 cm^3)
1 mark: t is proportional to sqrt(M): t(O2)/t(H2) = sqrt(32/2)
1 mark: = sqrt(16) = 4
1 mark: t(O2) = 4 x 20
1 mark: = 80 s
1 mark: Gas molecules collide continuously with the walls
1 mark: each collision changes their momentum, producing a force per unit area (pressure)
1 mark: Heating increases the average kinetic energy/speed of the molecules
1 mark: so they hit the walls more often and with greater force
1 mark: At high pressure molecules are close together
1 mark: so the volume of the molecules themselves is no longer negligible
1 mark: At low temperature molecules move slowly
1 mark: so intermolecular attractive forces become significant
1 mark: and the measured pressure/volume differs from the ideal value (gas may liquefy)
questions.explanation: (a) Random motion, negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions. (b) V proportional to T; rate inversely proportional to sqrt(M). (c) 179.6 cm^3. (d) 80 s. (e) Collisions with walls create pressure; heating makes collisions harder and more frequent. (f) Molecular volume and attractions are no longer negligible.

questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Rate of reaction: the change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time

2 marks: Temperature: particles move faster and more of them have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
2 marks: Surface area (particle size): smaller particles expose more surface for collisions
2 marks: Catalyst: provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are effective
2 marks: Light (for photochemical reactions): supplies energy to break bonds, e.g. H2 + Cl2, photosynthesis

1 mark: increasing the rate of decomposition without being used up

questions.stem:

(b) Name three air pollutants, state the source of each and one harmful effect. [9 marks]
(c) Explain how acid rain is formed and state two of its effects. [5 marks]
(d) State four ways of controlling water pollution in a Nigerian city. [4 marks]

questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances or energy into the environment, making it unsafe or unpleasant for living things
3 marks: Carbon(II) oxide: from incomplete combustion in vehicles and generators; combines with haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport (can cause death)
3 marks: Sulphur(IV) oxide: from burning fossil fuels containing sulphur; causes acid rain and respiratory problems
3 marks: Any other correct pollutant with source and effect, e.g. smoke/soot from bush burning (respiratory diseases) or CFCs from aerosols (ozone depletion) or nitrogen oxides from car engines (acid rain)
1 mark: SO2 and nitrogen oxides are released into the air
1 mark: they dissolve in rain water / are oxidised to form H2SO4 and HNO3
1 mark: the acidic rain falls to the ground
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: corrodes buildings and metal roofs; damages plants/forests; acidifies lakes and kills aquatic life; leaches nutrients from soil
4 marks: Any four, 1 mark each: proper treatment of sewage; treating industrial effluents before discharge; proper refuse disposal (not into drains/rivers); controlled use of fertilisers and pesticides; prevention of oil spills; public enlightenment and enforcement of laws
5 marks: Any five, 1 mark each: availability of raw materials; source of energy/power; transport facilities; market for products; availability of labour; water supply; government policy; waste disposal facilities
questions.explanation: (a) Introduction of harmful substances into the environment. (b) CO (vehicle exhaust, blocks haemoglobin), SO2 (fossil fuels, acid rain), soot (bush burning, respiratory disease). (c) SO2 and NOx dissolve in rain forming acids; corrode buildings, kill aquatic life. (d) Sewage treatment, effluent treatment, refuse disposal, laws. (e) Raw materials, power, transport, market, labour.

questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Fats and oils are esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) and long-chain fatty (alkanoic) acids
1 mark: (triglycerides)
1 mark: Fats are solid at room temperature and are mainly saturated (largely from animals)
1 mark: Oils are liquid at room temperature and are mainly unsaturated (largely from plants)
1 mark: Boil palm oil with concentrated sodium hydroxide (or potassium hydroxide) solution
1 mark: Stir continuously for some time until the mixture becomes homogeneous
1 mark: Add concentrated sodium chloride solution (salting out)
1 mark: Soap separates and floats on top
1 mark: Skim off the soap, wash and allow to harden (perfume/colour may be added)
2 marks: Palm oil + sodium hydroxide -> soap (sodium salt of fatty acids) + glycerol
1 mark: Hard water contains Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ ions
1 mark: which react with soap to form insoluble scum, wasting soap
1 mark: Soapless detergents (e.g. sodium alkylbenzene sulphonates) do not form scum
1 mark: because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble
1 mark: Starch: glucose
1 mark: Proteins: amino acids
2 marks: Sucrose: glucose and fructose
1 mark: Starch: add iodine solution
1 mark: Blue-black colour
1 mark: Protein: add NaOH solution and a few drops of dilute CuSO4 (Biuret test) or Millon's reagent
1 mark: Violet/purple colour (or red/pink with Millon's on warming)
1 mark: Reducing sugar: warm with Fehling's (or Benedict's) solution
1 mark: Brick-red precipitate

questions.stem:
(a) Explain why (i) aluminium is extracted by electrolysis while iron is extracted by reduction with carbon; (ii) metals generally occur in nature as compounds. [4 marks]
(b) Describe the extraction of iron from haematite in the blast furnace. Give equations for the main reactions and state the function of limestone. [10 marks]
(c) Calculate the mass of iron that can be obtained from 1 000 kg of an ore containing 80% Fe2O3 by mass. (Fe = 56, O = 16) [4 marks]
(d) What are alloys? Name two alloys of iron or copper and give one use of each. [5 marks]
(e) A solution of a salt gives a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation present. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series; its oxide is too stable to be reduced by carbon
1 mark: Iron is lower in the series, so its oxide is reduced by carbon/CO cheaply
1 mark: Most metals are reactive
1 mark: and combine with oxygen, sulphur, carbonate etc. in the environment (only unreactive metals like gold occur free)
1 mark: Charge: iron ore (haematite), coke and limestone fed in at the top
1 mark: Hot air blown in at the bottom
1 mark: Coke burns: C + O2 -> CO2 (provides heat)
1 mark: CO2 + C -> 2CO
2 marks: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (reduction of the ore)
1 mark: Limestone decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
1 mark: CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (slag)
1 mark: Function of limestone: removes silica (acidic impurities) as slag
1 mark: Molten iron and slag are tapped off separately at the bottom (slag floats on iron)
1 mark: M(Fe2O3) = 160; mass of Fe2O3 = 0.80 x 1000 = 800 kg
1 mark: 160 kg Fe2O3 gives 112 kg Fe
1 mark: mass = 800 x 112/160
1 mark: = 560 kg
1 mark: Alloy: a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals) to improve properties
2 marks: First alloy with use, e.g. steel (iron and carbon) - construction/tools; stainless steel - cutlery
2 marks: Second alloy with use, e.g. brass (copper and zinc) - ornaments, fittings; bronze (copper and tin) - medals, statues
2 marks: Iron(III) ion, Fe^3+ (precipitate is Fe(OH)3)
questions.explanation: (a) Al oxide too stable for carbon; metals are reactive and occur combined. (b) Coke burns to CO2 then CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2; limestone forms CaO which removes SiO2 as CaSiO3 slag. (c) 560 kg. (d) Mixtures of metals: steel (construction), brass (fittings). (e) Fe^3+.
